briefs.solution: A version-based workflow letting managers edit a signed document by creating a new version that goes through re-approval, while the original signed version is retained.

a re-approval trigger distinct from initial approval, layered onto the existing approval-circuit engine

challenges.headline: "Edit and re-approve" as a simple action
challenges.premise: The request treats editing a signed document as a straightforward edit-then-reapprove step.
challenges.alternative: Model it explicitly as version supersession: the edit creates a new version, the signed version is retained and stamped superseded, and re-approval applies only to the new version — never to the frozen original.
challenges.consequence: Without this, either the signed content gets mutated in place (destroying the audit trail and invalidating the original signature silently) or the team improvises versioning mid-build, which is expensive to retrofit.
challenges.recommendation: Define the supersession rule (new version, retained original, invalidated signature) as the core mechanic before scoping the rest of the workflow.

challenges.headline: Re-approval vs. what readers see
challenges.premise: The request implies that once re-approved, the document simply 'becomes valid again,' without saying what happens to the version currently published and read by others while the edit is mid-approval.
challenges.alternative: Keep the currently published version live and marked 'current' throughout the re-approval, and only swap it for the new version once approval completes — never let a mid-approval draft become the version people act on.
challenges.consequence: Conflating approval status with publication status is the classic failure mode here: readers could end up viewing an unapproved edit, or the live version could go missing while approval is pending.
challenges.recommendation: Design the approval-lifecycle / publication-lifecycle interaction explicitly, with the client, before implementation.

challenges.headline: Unscoped manager edit rights
challenges.premise: The request names 'managers' as the actor who may edit and re-approve, without defining whether that means the document owner, the original approver, or any manager, and without addressing documents that are under legal hold or already filed/exported.
challenges.alternative: Scope edit rights to the document owner or original approver, and block or specially log edit attempts on documents under legal hold or already exported — protecting compliance while still allowing genuine corrections.
challenges.consequence: An unscoped 'any manager can edit' rule combined with no retention check risks a compliance breach: someone could alter a legally held or already-filed signed document.
challenges.recommendation: Validate actor scope and the legal-hold/retention interaction with compliance stakeholders before estimating the build.

decisions.tradeoff: Added versioning and data-model complexity, in exchange for a signed record that stays valid and referenceable.

decisions.decision: The edit-and-re-approval action will carry a full audit trail (who edited, what changed, full re-approval history).

briefs.solution: A versioning/supersession flow that lets a manager edit a signed document by creating a new draft version, routes it through re-approval, and retains the original as a superseded, still-referenceable record.

challenges.headline: Re-approval circuit assumed identical
challenges.premise: The request implicitly treats 're-approve' as reusing the same signatories and circuit as the original signature.
challenges.alternative: A distinct, possibly lighter, re-approval circuit — configurable per client or per change type — avoids forcing every content correction through the full original signatory list, some of whom may no longer be reachable.
challenges.consequence: If the original signatories must always re-sign, an unavailable signatory blocks a correction indefinitely, and the approval engine now needs a second circuit shape it wasn't built for.
challenges.recommendation: Confirm with the client whether re-approval reuses the original circuit, uses a lighter one, or is configurable, before building the routing logic.

challenges.headline: Auto-republish on re-approval
challenges.premise: The flow reads as if a re-approved version automatically becomes the published/current one that readers see.
challenges.alternative: Keep publication a separate, manual step — consistent with the platform's own two-lifecycle model — so approval and 'what readers currently see' stay decoupled.
challenges.consequence: Conflating approved with published is the platform's own named trap: readers could silently start acting on a new version before anyone reviewed or communicated the change.
challenges.recommendation: Explicitly design publication as its own controlled step and confirm with the client whether it should auto-publish or wait for a deliberate action.

challenges.headline: Unscoped manager edit rights
challenges.premise: Only the role 'manager' is named as able to edit signed documents, with no stated boundary on which documents.
challenges.alternative: Scope edit rights by ownership, department or classification, in line with the platform's classification-driven access model, rather than a blanket 'any manager, any document' rule.
challenges.consequence: An unscoped edit right lets managers modify documents outside their remit, undermining classification-based access control — exactly the kind of gap the context card flags as usually caught only at acceptance testing.
challenges.recommendation: Define and confirm the edit-permission scope with the client before implementation.

briefs.solution: A controlled edit-and-re-approve flow for signed documents that creates a new version, re-runs an approval circuit, and keeps the prior signed version retained and correctly flagged.

challenges.headline: Old version pulled during re-approval
challenges.premise: The request implies an edit simply replaces the signed document, without stating what stays visible/live while re-approval is pending.
challenges.alternative: Keep the previously signed version as the current/published one until the new version completes re-approval — this is exactly the approved-vs-published distinction the platform already models.
challenges.consequence: If the old version is taken down the moment editing starts, anyone referencing the document — internally or downstream — loses access to any valid version for the entire re-approval window, which is a legal and operational gap, not just a UX one.
challenges.recommendation: Decide explicitly that publication state stays on the old version until the new one is approved, and surface a visible 'pending re-approval' state.

challenges.headline: Every edit forces full re-signature
challenges.premise: The request treats 'edit and re-approve' as one uniform action, implying any change — trivial or substantive — triggers the full original approval/signature circuit.
challenges.alternative: Distinguish correction-level changes from substantive changes, and route only substantive ones through full re-signature — the same logic the platform already applies to amendments versus in-place edits elsewhere.
challenges.consequence: Without this distinction, a one-word typo fix costs as much process as a full renegotiation, which will push managers to work around the system rather than through it — defeating the audit trail the feature exists to provide.
challenges.recommendation: Work with compliance/legal to define what counts as a substantive change before building the re-approval trigger logic.

challenges.headline: Unscoped manager edit rights
challenges.premise: The request names 'managers' as the actor who can edit signed documents, with no stated limit on which documents.
challenges.alternative: Scope edit rights by ownership, department or classification tier, mirroring the platform's classification-driven access model rather than a blanket role check.
challenges.consequence: An unscoped rule lets any manager alter a signed, potentially confidential document outside their remit — a compliance exposure and a far larger permission surface to build and test than intended.
challenges.recommendation: Confirm the document scope (ownership, classification, document type) the edit right applies to before estimating the permission work.

If edit rights aren't scoped by classification, this bypasses the platform's access-control model and could surface confidential content to the wrong manager.

opportunities.text: Generalize the supersession + re-approval flow into a reusable 'amend a signed artifact' capability rather than a one-off feature bolted onto Document.
Extend the existing configurable-approval-circuit mechanism to support re-approval variants, instead of building a parallel circuit definition.
Design the audit trail schema for this feature so it can also serve future controlled-change events (e.g. reclassification, retention override) rather than a single-purpose log.

next_steps: Confirm with the client whether all edits require full re-signature or only substantive ones, and define that threshold.
Decide what stays 'current/published' during the re-approval window before touching the publication state model.
Scope exactly which documents and which managers this edit right applies to (ownership, classification, department).
Design the audit trail (edit diff, invalidated/re-collected signatures, re-approval history) before building the versioning path, not after.

decisions.decision: Editing a signed document always produces a new Version rather than mutating the frozen one, consistent with the platform's frozen-after-approval standard.
